2026-Q01.shortcut: Row sums of |x+y| for x = -2,-1,0,1,2 are 10, 7, 6, 7, 10, total 40, so $c = 1/40$ and $\operatorname{P}(X) = (0.25, 0.175, 0.15, 0.175, 0.25)$. Symmetry gives $\operatorname{E}(X) = 0$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^{2}) = 2(4)(0.25) + 2(1)(0.175) = 2 + 0.35 = 2.35$.
tips: Get c first: the number of pairs summing to s is 5 - |s| for |s| <= 4, so sum |x+y| = $2(4 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 4) = 40$ and $c = 1/40$.
The marginal row sums 10, 7, 6, 7, 10 are symmetric about $x = 0$, which forces $\operatorname{E}(X) = 0$ and turns the variance into a pure $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$ computation.
Only x = +/-2 and x = +/-1 contribute to $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$; $x = 0$ contributes nothing, so it is a two-term sum.
The same marginal serves for Y by symmetry, so $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 2.35$ as well - handy if a companion question asks for it.
solution: Normalising constant: sum over x, y in {-2,-1,0,1,2} of |x + y|. The number of pairs with $x + y = s$ is 5 - |s|, so the total is $4(1) + 3(2) + 2(3) + 1(4) + 0(5) + 1(4) + 2(3) + 3(2) + 4(1) = 40$. Hence $c = 1/40$.
Marginal of X: $\operatorname{P}(X = x) = (1/40) * \sum \mid x + y$|.

2026-Q02.shortcut: Along the row $X = 1$ the weights |1+y| for y = -2,-1,0,1,2 are 1, 0, 1, 2, 3 with total 7. So $\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X=1) = [(-2)(1) + (-1)(0) + 0(1) + 1(2) + 2(3)]/7 = 6/7$.
tips: For a conditional expectation on a discrete grid, work with the unnormalised row weights and divide by the row total once at the end - the constant c cancels.
The row total 7 is exactly the marginal weight $\operatorname{P}(X = 1) = 7/40$ found in the previous part; reuse it rather than recomputing.
Note that |1 + y| = 0 at y = -1, so that term drops out entirely.
Sanity check the sign: the row weights are heavier on the positive y side (2 and 3 versus 1 and 0), so $\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X=1)$ must be positive, ruling out any negative answer.
solution: The joint weights along the row $X = 1$ are $\operatorname{P}(X = 1, Y = y)$ = |1 + y|/40.
Conditional pmf: $\operatorname{P}(Y = y \mid X = 1)$ = |1 + y|/7, giving $1/7, 0, 1/7, 2/7, 3/7$ for y = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2.

2026-Q03.shortcut: |x - y| <= 1 means the main diagonal plus the two adjacent diagonals. Weights: diagonal |2x| gives $4+2+0+2+4 = 12$; each off-diagonal gives $3+1+1+3 = 8$. Total $12 + 8 + 8 = 28$, so $P = 28/40 = 0.7$.
tips: Organise the 25 cells by diagonals: on $y = x$ the weight is |2x|, on $y = x+1$ it is |2x+1|, on $y = x-1$ it is |2x-1|. Each diagonal is then a four- or five-term sum.
The two off-diagonals give the same total by the symmetry of the weight in x and y - compute one and double it.
Always divide by 40, not by 25: the distribution is not uniform on the grid.
0.7 and 0.3 are complements, and $0.06 / 0.12$ are far too small to be a 13-cell event - a quick magnitude check rules them out.
solution: The event |X - Y| <= 1 covers the cells with $y = x, y = x + 1$ and $y = x - 1$, i.e. $5 + 4 + 4 = 13$ of the 25 cells.
Cells with $y = x$: weight |x + y| = |2x| = 4, 2, 0, 2, 4 for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, total 12.

2026-Q04.shortcut: The standard normal density is symmetric about 0, so $\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)$ for every z. Put $z = 100$. Answer (b).
tips: Memorise the symmetry relation $\Phi(-z) + \Phi(z) = 1$; it is the single most-used property of the standard normal CDF.
A CDF can never be negative, so option (a) is impossible on sight.
Option (d) would give a negative number since $\Phi(100)$ is essentially 1; another instant rejection.
Numerically $\Phi(-100)$ is about $10^{-2174}$, i.e. effectively 0, consistent with $1 - \Phi(100)$.
solution: By definition $\Phi(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_{X}(\theta) d \theta$, where $f_{X}$ is the $N(0,1)$ density.
Substituting $\theta$ = -u in the integral for $\Phi(-z)$ gives $\Phi(-z) = \int_{z}^{\infty} f_{X}(u)\,du = 1 - \Phi(z)$.
Options (a) and (d) would be negative (since $\Phi(100)$ is essentially 1), which is impossible for a CDF; option (c) contradicts the symmetry relation.

2026-Q05.shortcut: The inner integral $g(y) = \int_{-y}^{y} f_{X} = \Phi(y) - \Phi(-y)$ is an odd function of y, and the outer range $[-10, 10]$ is symmetric about 0. An odd function integrated over a symmetric interval gives 0.
tips: Do the inner integral symbolically first - here it collapses to $2\Phi(y) - 1$, whose oddness is the whole point.
Check oddness explicitly: $g(-y) = \Phi(-y) - \Phi(y)$ = -g(y). Do not assume the inner integral is automatically non-negative just because $f_{X}$ is.
When $y < 0$ the limits -y to y run backwards, so the inner integral is negative - this is the step most candidates miss, which is why $1/2$ is the popular wrong answer.
General principle: $\int_{-a}^{a}$ an odd function is 0; $\int_{-a}^{a}$ an even function is 2 * integral from 0 to a.
solution: Then $g(-y) = 2 \Phi(-y) - 1 = 2(1 - \Phi(y)) - 1 = 1 - 2 \Phi(y)$ = -g(y), so g is an odd function of y.
The required double integral is $\int_{-10}^{10} g(y)\,dy$.
An odd integrable function integrated over an interval symmetric about the origin gives 0: the contribution from y in $(0, 10)$ exactly cancels that from y in $(-10, 0)$.

tips: The marginal at $y = 0.5$ evaluating to exactly 1 is the designed simplification - the conditional density is then just the joint density with y substituted.
Substitute $y = 0.5$ before integrating, not after; carrying a symbolic y through doubles the work.
Verify the conditional integrates to 1: $\int_{0}^{1} 2(x+1)/3\,dx = (2/3)(1/2 + 1) = 1$. A ten-second check that catches algebra slips.
Since the conditional density increases in $x, \operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = 0.5)$ must exceed $1/2$ - that alone eliminates options (a) and (b).
Reuse the conditional density and the conditional mean from the previous part; only $\operatorname{E}(X^{2} \mid Y = 0.5)$ is new work.
Convert to the common denominator 162 immediately: $7/18 = 63/162$ and $25/81 = 50/162$, so the subtraction is a single step.

Sanity bound: X lies in $(0,1)$, so its conditional variance cannot exceed $1/4 = 40.5/162$; $13/162 = 0.080$ is comfortably inside, and even the uniform value $1/12 = 13.5/162$ is close, as expected for a gently sloping density.
The distractors $11/162, 5/54 = 15/162$ and $17/162$ all come from small slips in $\operatorname{E}(X^{2})$ or in squaring $5/9$ - keep fractions exact throughout.
solution: From the previous part, $f(x \mid Y = 0.5) = 2(x + 1)/3$ on $0 < x < 1$, with $\operatorname{E}(X \mid Y = 0.5) = 5/9$.

2026-Q08.shortcut: Integrate out y over $(0,2)$: $f_{X}(x) = 2x^{2} + 2x/3 = (2x/3)(3x + 1)$. Dividing the joint by this cancels the x, leaving $(3x + y)/[2(3x + 1)]$. Option (a).
tips: Conditional of Y given X means divide by the marginal of X, so integrate the joint over the y-range - keep track of which variable is being eliminated.
Factor the joint as $x(3x + y)/3$ before dividing; the common factor x then cancels visibly and the answer's shape becomes obvious.

Elimination test: for a valid conditional density of Y given X, integrating over $0 < y < 2$ must give 1. Option (a): $\int (3x+y)/[2(3x+1)]\,dy = (6x + 2)/[2(3x+1)] = 1$. It passes; the others do not.
The conditional pdf of Y given X must not have a stray free x that fails to normalise - options (b), (c), (d) all break the normalisation check.
solution: Joint density factored: $f(x, y) = x^{2} + xy/3 = (x/3)(3x + y)$.

2026-Q09.shortcut: $f_{Y}(y) = \int_{0}^{1} (x^{2} + xy/3)\,dx = 1/3 + y/6 = (2 + y)/6$. Dividing the joint by this gives $6(x^{2} + xy/3)/(2+y) = 2x(3x + y)/(2 + y)$. Option (c).
tips: Now integrate out x over $(0,1)$ - the opposite variable from the previous part; mixing the two up is the classic error.
Write the marginal as a single fraction $(2 + y)/6$ before dividing, so the factor 6 comes up cleanly in the numerator.
Normalisation check: $\int_{0}^{1} 2x(3x+y)/(2+y)\,dx = (2 + y)/(2 + y) = 1$. Option (c) passes; test the others the same way and they fail.
Compare with the previous answer: the conditional of Y given X kept x in the denominator's shape, whereas this one keeps y - a useful structural cross-check.
solution: Conditional density: $f(x \mid y) = f(x, y)/f_{Y}(y) = (x^{2} + xy/3) \cdot 6/(2 + y) = (6x^{2} + 2xy)/(2 + y) = 2x(3x + y)/(2 + y)$, for $0 < x < 1, 0 < y < 2$.

2026-Q10.issue: The answer depends on the counting convention. Using the standard Indian-textbook convention in which both the geometric and the negative binomial count FAILURES (geometric mean $q/p$, negative binomial mean rq/p), $\operatorname{E}(X) = \operatorname{E}(Y) = 1$ and $2 = 3(1-p)/p$ gives $p = 3/5$, option (d). If instead both are taken as counting TRIALS (means $1/p$ and $r/p$), then $4 = 3/p$ gives $p = 3/4$, option (b), which is why both values appear among the choices. Option (d) is keyed here on the failure-counting convention; a candidate should state the convention used.
2026-Q10.shortcut: With the failure-counting convention, geometric($1/2$) has mean $q/p = 1$, so $\operatorname{E}(X + Y) = 2$, and NB(3, p) has mean $3q/p$. Set $3(1 - p)/p = 2$ to get $5p = 3, p = 3/5$.
tips: State your convention before computing: geometric as number of failures has mean $q/p$; as number of trials it has mean $1/p$. The same split applies to the negative binomial (rq/p versus $r/p$).
Whichever convention you adopt, use it for BOTH distributions - the geometric is the negative binomial with $r = 1$, so mixing conventions is internally inconsistent.

Expectation is linear whether or not the variables are independent, so $\operatorname{E}(X + Y - Z) = \operatorname{E}(X) + \operatorname{E}(Y) - \operatorname{E}(Z)$; the stated independence is needed only if a variance were asked.
The two consistent conventions produce exactly the two 'nice' options $3/5$ and $3/4$ - recognising that tells you which pair of distractors are decoys.
solution: Adopt the standard convention in which the geometric variable counts the number of failures before the first success: $\operatorname{P}(X = x) = q^{x} p, x = 0, 1, 2$, ..., with $\operatorname{E}(X) = q/p$.

Under the matching convention, the negative binomial with parameters $r = 3$ and p counts the failures before the 3rd success: $\operatorname{P}(Z = z) = \binom{z + 2}{z} p^{3} q^{z}$, with $\operatorname{E}(Z) = 3q/p = 3(1 - p)/p$.
Hence option (d) is correct under the failure-counting convention; see the note above for the trials convention.

2026-Q11.shortcut: The ratio of two independent standard normals is the standard Cauchy - a memorised standard result. Answer (b).
tips: Memorise the family: X/Y is Cauchy(0,1); $X^{2}/Y^{2}$ is $F(1,1)$; $X^{2} + Y^{2}$ is $\chi^{2}$ with 2 df; X/|Y| is also Cauchy.
Option (d) is the trap: $F(1,1)$ is the distribution of the ratio of SQUARES, not of the variables themselves.
The Cauchy has no mean and no variance, which is why the ratio of two well-behaved normals is famously pathological - a favourite examiner point.
Cauchy(0,1) has density $1/[pi(1 + z^{2})]$ on the whole real line; the location 0 and scale 1 follow from both normals having mean 0 and variance 1, so (c) with location 1 is wrong.
solution: Let $Z = X/Y$ with X, Y independent $N(0,1)$.
Using the transformation $Z = X/Y, W = Y$ with Jacobian |w|, the joint density of (Z, W) is |w| * $(1/(2pi)) \exp(-(z^{2} w^{2} + w^{2})/2)$.
Integrating out w: $f_{Z}(z) = (1/(2pi)) * \int \lvert w\rvert \exp(-w^{2}(1 + z^{2})/2)\,dw = (1/(2pi)) \cdot 2/(1 + z^{2}) = 1/[pi(1 + z^{2})]$.
This is exactly the standard Cauchy density, i.e. Cauchy with location 0 and scale 1.
$\chi^{2}$ with 2 df (option a) is the distribution of $X^{2} + Y^{2}$, not X/Y; $F(1,1)$ (option d) is the distribution of $X^{2}/Y^{2}$; Cauchy(1,1) (option c) has the wrong location parameter.

2026-Q12.shortcut: The prior $1/3$ cancels, so the posterior is just $3/8$ divided by $(2/5 + 3/8 + 5/7)$. Over LCD 280 these are 112, 105 and 200, total 417. Answer $105/417 = 35/139$.
tips: When all priors are equal they cancel in Bayes' formula - the posterior is simply the likelihood divided by the sum of the likelihoods.
Put the three white-ball probabilities over a common denominator (280 here) at once; the numerators 112, 105, 200 then make the arithmetic exact.
Always reduce: $105/417$ has common factor 3, giving $35/139$. The unreduced form is deliberately absent, and $112/417$ is the answer for urn 1 while $200/417$ is for urn 3.
Cross-check: the three posteriors $112/417, 105/417$ and $200/417$ must sum to 1 - they do.
solution: Let U1, U2, U3 be the events that urn 1, 2, 3 is chosen, each with prior probability $1/3$, and let W be the event that the drawn ball is white.
Over the common denominator 280: $2/5 = 112/280, 3/8 = 105/280, 5/7 = 200/280$, so the sum is $417/280$ and $\operatorname{P}(W) = 417/840$.

2026-Q13.shortcut: $b(Y on X) = \rho * \sigma_{y}/\sigma_{x} = 0.6 \cdot (3/4) = 0.45 = 9/20$. The means 5 and 8 are irrelevant.
tips: Take square roots first: $\sigma_{x} = 4$ and $\sigma_{y} = 3$ from the variances 16 and 9. Using the variances directly is the standard trap and would give $0.6 \cdot (9/16) = 27/80$.
Y on X puts $\sigma_{y}$ on top: $b_{yx} = \rho \sigma_{y}/\sigma_{x}$. X on Y flips it: $b_{xy} = \rho \sigma_{x}/\sigma_{y} = 0.6(4/3) = 0.8$.
Check: $b_{yx} \cdot b_{xy} = \rho^{2}$, so $0.45 \cdot 0.8 = 0.36 = 0.6^{2}$. A five-second confirmation.
The means $\mu_{x}$ and $\mu_{y}$ affect only the intercept of the regression line, never the slope - ignore them here.
solution: For a bivariate normal distribution, the regression of Y on X is linear: $\operatorname{E}(Y \mid X = x) = \mu_{y} + \rho (\sigma_{y}/\sigma_{x})(x - \mu_{x})$.
The regression coefficient of Y on X is therefore $b_{yx} = \rho * \sigma_{y} / \sigma_{x}$.
Check with the reverse coefficient: $b_{xy} = 0.6 \cdot (4/3) = 0.8$, and $b_{yx} \cdot b_{xy} = 0.45 \cdot 0.8 = 0.36 = \rho^{2}$, as required.

2026-Q14.shortcut: Constant density on [a, b] means X is uniform, whose variance is $(b-a)^{2}/12$, so the SD is $(b-a)/(2 sqrt 3)$. Answer (b).
tips: 'Density constant on an interval and zero elsewhere' is the definition of the continuous uniform distribution - recognise the phrasing.
Uniform facts: mean $(a+b)/2$, variance $(b-a)^{2}/12$, and $\sqrt{12} = 2 sqrt 3$.
Options (c) and (d) are the mean and the half-range respectively - both are spread or location quantities, but neither is the SD.
A standard deviation must be translation invariant, i.e. it can depend only on b - a, not on a + b. That instantly kills options (a) and (c).
solution: If the density is constant on $a \le x \le b$ and zero elsewhere, then $f(x) = 1/(b - a)$ on [a, b], i.e. X follows the uniform distribution U(a, b).

2026-Q15.shortcut: Drop $x = 1$ and renormalise. The 15 in the denominator cancels, so $\operatorname{E}(X \mid X > 1) = (2^{2} + 3^{2} + 4^{2} + 5^{2})/(2 + 3 + 4 + 5) = 54/14 = 27/7$.
tips: For a conditional expectation on a truncated support, take the ratio of unnormalised sums - the common denominator (15 here) cancels.
Numerator terms are x * p(x) proportional to $x \cdot x = x^{2}$; denominator terms are p(x) proportional to x. Recognising this turns the problem into sum of squares over sum.
Check the pmf is valid: $(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5)/15 = 1$, so $p(x) = x/15$ is proper.
Bound check: conditioning on $X > 1$ must raise the mean above the unconditional $\operatorname{E}(X) = 55/15 = 11/3 = 3.67$; $27/7 = 3.857$ is above it, while $15/7$ and $15/14$ are far too small.
solution: The pmf is $p(x) = x/15$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ (check: sum = $15/15 = 1$).

2026-Q16.shortcut: Intersect the events first: $(5, 7)$ intersect $(6, 12) = (6, 7)$, of length 1. Divide by the length of the conditioning event $(6, 12)$, which is 6. Answer $1/6$.
tips: For a uniform variable, conditional probability is just a ratio of interval lengths - no integration needed.
Always intersect before dividing: the numerator is P($5 < X < 7$ AND $X > 6$) = $\operatorname{P}(6 < X < 7)$, not $\operatorname{P}(5 < X < 7) = 2/12$.
The distractor $1/3$ comes from forgetting the intersection: $(2/12)/(6/12) = 1/3$. This is the single most common error on this item.
General identity: $\operatorname{P}(A \mid B) = \operatorname{P}\!\left(A\ \text{intersect B}\right)/\operatorname{P}(B)$, valid whenever $\operatorname{P}(B) > 0$.
solution: X is uniform on $(0, 12)$ with density $1/12$, so probabilities are proportional to interval lengths.

2026-Q17.shortcut: Add the expansions of $(q + p)^{n}$ and $(q - p)^{n}$: odd terms cancel and even terms double. So the sum of even-index terms is $[1 + (q - p)^{n}]/2$. Answer (b).
tips: The even/odd splitting trick: sum of even terms = $[f(1) + f(-1)]/2$ and sum of odd terms = $[f(1) - f(-1)]/2$, applied to the pgf.
Here $f(s) = (q + ps)^{n}$, so $f(1) = 1$ and $f(-1) = (q - p)^{n}$. That is the entire derivation.
Sanity check with $n = 1$: $\operatorname{P}(X = 0) = q$, and the formula gives $[1 + (q - p)]/2 = (1 + q - p)/2 = (q + q)/2 = q$ since $p + q = 1$. Correct.
Options (a) and (d) can exceed 1 (take $p = 0$, giving 2 and 2 respectively), so they are impossible probabilities; option (c) is the odd-count probability.
solution: $\operatorname{P}(X = x) = \binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x}$. We want $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X\ \text{is even, including 0}\right)$ = sum over even x of $\binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x}$.
Consider the binomial expansions $(q + p)^{n} = \sum \binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x} = 1$, and $(q - p)^{n} = \sum \binom{n}{x} (-p)^{x} q^{n-x} = \sum (-1)^{x} \binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x}$.
Adding the two: the terms with odd x cancel and the terms with even x double.
So $(q + p)^{n} + (q - p)^{n} = 2$ * sum over even x of $\binom{n}{x} p^{x} q^{n-x}$.

Verification at $n = 1$: $[1 + q - p]/2 = q = \operatorname{P}(X = 0)$, correct. (Correspondingly $\operatorname{P}\!\left(X\ \text{odd}\right) = [1 - (q - p)^{n}]/2$, which is option (c) - a deliberate distractor.)

2026-Q18.shortcut: Condition on N: $\operatorname{E}(e^{tS_N}) = \operatorname{E}[(M_{X}(t))^{N}] = \operatorname{E}[e^{N \log M_{X}(t)}] = M_{N}(\log M_{X}(t))$. Answer (b).
tips: The compounding rule: for a random sum, the outer MGF is evaluated at $\log$ of the inner MGF - $M_{S_N}(t) = M_{N}(\log M_{X}(t))$.
In pgf language it is cleaner still: $P_{S_N}(s) = P_{N}(P_{X}(s)) - a$ straight composition, with no logarithm.
Derivation in one line: $\operatorname{E}[a^{N}] = M_{N}(\log a)$ with $a = M_{X}(t)$, by writing $a^{N} = e^{N \log a}$.
Standard application: if N is Poisson($\lambda$) then $M_{S_N}(t) = \exp(\lambda[M_{X}(t) - 1])$, the compound Poisson MGF - a frequent follow-up question.
solution: By the law of total expectation, $M_{S_N}(t) = \operatorname{E}[e^{t S_N}] = \operatorname{E}[ \operatorname{E}(e^{t S_N} \mid N) ]$.
Given $N = n, S_{N}$ is the sum of n iid copies of $X_{1}$, so $\operatorname{E}(e^{t S_N} \mid N = n) = [M_{X_1}(t)]^{n}$ by independence.
Write $a = M_{X_1}(t) > 0$. Then $a^{N} = e^{N \log a}$, so $\operatorname{E}[a^{N}] = \operatorname{E}[e^{N \log a}] = M_{N}(\log a)$.
Check with N Poisson($\lambda$): $M_{N}(u) = \exp(\lambda(e^{u} - 1))$, so $M_{S_N}(t) = \exp(\lambda(M_{X_1}(t) - 1))$, the standard compound Poisson result.

tips: Sketch the region first: $y = x^{2}$ is the lower boundary and $y = 1$ the upper; the line $y = x$ cuts it, and on $(0,1)$ we have $x^{2} \le x$, so the y-limits are $x^{2}$ to x.
Do the y-integral first (it is a plain power of y), leaving a single polynomial integral in x.
Verify the constant: integral over the full support gives $(21/4)(1/3 - 1/7) = (21/4)(4/21) = 1$, so $21/2$ is right and your limits are set up correctly.
Note 0.7 is the complement $\operatorname{P}(X < Y)$; read the inequality direction carefully before choosing.
solution: The density $f(x, y) = (21/2) x^{2} y$ is supported on {$0 < x < 1, x^{2} \le y \le 1$}.
For $\operatorname{P}(X \ge Y)$ we need $y \le x$, and combined with the support $y \ge x^{2}$ the y-range is $x^{2} \le y \le x$ (valid since $x^{2} \le x$ for $0 < x < 1$).

2026-Q20.shortcut: Real roots need discriminant $X^{2} - 4Y \ge 0$, i.e. $Y \le X^{2}/4$. Since $X^{2}/4 \le 9$ on $(0,6)$, the favourable area is $\int_{0}^{6} x^{2}/4\,dx = 18$, out of the total area $6 \cdot 9 = 54$. So $P = 18/54 = 1/3$.
tips: Geometric probability: with X and Y independent uniforms, the probability is (favourable area)/(total area) of the rectangle - no densities needed beyond the constant $1/54$.

Check whether the curve leaves the rectangle: $y = x^{2}/4$ reaches 9 exactly at $x = 6$, so the parabola stays inside and no truncation ($\min$ with 9) is needed. Getting this wrong is the usual pitfall.
The condition for real roots of $z^{2}$ - Xz + $Y = 0$ is $X^{2} \ge 4Y$; note the sign convention $b^{2} - 4$ac with $a = 1, b$ = -$X, c = Y$.
Area under a parabola: $\int_{0}^{6} x^{2}/4\,dx = 6^{3}/12 = 18$. Memorising $\int x^{2} = x^{3}/3$ makes this instant.
solution: X is uniform on $(0, 6)$ and Y is uniform on $(0, 9)$, independently, so (X, Y) is uniform on the rectangle of area $6 \cdot 9 = 54$, with joint density $1/54$.
The quadratic $Z^{2}$ - XZ + $Y = 0$ has real roots iff its discriminant is non-negative: $X^{2} - 4Y \ge 0$, i.e. $Y \le X^{2}/4$.
For $0 < x < 6$ the bound $x^{2}/4$ ranges from 0 up to $36/4 = 9$, which is exactly the top of the Y-range, so the parabola lies entirely within the rectangle and no truncation is needed.
